newsitem.title: USA: U.S. failing in push to enlist allies on Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. failing in push to enlist allies on Cuba.

text.p: The United States acknowledged on Wednesday that efforts to get allies to join a democracy and human rights initiative on Cuba have so far failed.
Last July, President Bill Clinton ordered the anti-Cuba trade law known as Helms-Burton to come into force but delayed implementation for six months to appease U.S. allies who threatened retaliation.

Clinton also appointed Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat to try to placate the allies and persuade them to make common cause in pressuring Cuban leader Fidel Castro to make democratic, human rights and economic reforms.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, however, said on Wednesday that Washington had not made progress despite two months of work by Eisenstat with all countries who have objected to Helms-Burton.
"I cannot point to any specific initiative that these countries have agreed to undertake with us, no."
He said the only progress was in "raising the consciousness of some of these countries on this issue."

Nevertheless, Burns insisted: "I frankly think it's too early to judge what the result of our conversations with Canada and Mexico and the European countries will be." He said Eizenstat would continue his efforts on the issue.

The Helms-Burton law, named after two legislators, allows lawsuits to be filed in U.S. courts against foreign firms that own or operate properties confiscated by Cuba after its 1959 Communist revolution from U.S. citizens or Cubans who are now U.S. citizens.
The law also allows the denial of visas to shareholders and officers of foreign firms operating these properties in Cuba.
In his talks with Europe, Canada and Mexico, Eizenstat stressed the U.S. commitment to miminize the effect of the anti-Cuba law on allies and maximize the impact on Castro.

The administration has held out the possibility that Clinton could show flexibility on the lawsuits issue in February 1997 if the allies cooperate in pressuring Cuba on human rights, democracy and economic reforms.

Burns said another message carried by Eizenstat was: "We can agree to disagree on the issue of Helms-Burton and the sanctions ... put in place by the Congress in Helms-Burton. But we should not disagree on the issue of human rights in Cuba."

"And it would be good to see at least some attention given to that issue by some of our European friends and by Canada and Mexico because Cuba is the last remaining autocracy in this hemisphere," he added.

Two Canadian parliamentarians have introduced legislation that mockingly suggests Canadians deserve compensation for lands seized from their Tory ancestors in the American Revolution, including land where the White House stands.
But the anger behind the bill is no joke. Canada is Cuba's biggest trading partner, active in tourism, mining and other sectors, and is furious over Helms-Burton.
Burns ridiculed the Canadian parody of Helms-Burton, whimsically citing past offences against the United States, like burning the White House in the War of 1812.

"I'll make a promise that in reaction to this, the United States will not insist that Canada pay up for its participation as part of the British Empire, for the burning of the White House in 1812," he said.

"And we certainly won't talk about the wrongful use of force by the British Empire in March of 1770 in Boston, Massachusetts, during the Boston Massacre ... I think we'll just probably derive most of our satisfaction from the fact that the United States defeated Canada in the last World Cup."
On a serious note, he said Canadians should get beyond Helms-Burton and make Cuban human rights a priority.
